name: Amos
title: The Prophet of Justice from Tekoa
summary: Amos was a shepherd and a grower of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah who was called by God to prophesy against the northern kingdom of Israel during the prosperous reign of King Jeroboam II. He was not a professional prophet, but an ordinary person who preached powerfully against social injustice, oppression of the poor, corrupt justice systems, and empty religion. Amos' core message was that God demands true justice and mercy, not merely outward rituals and sacrifices. His prophecies, dated "two years before the earthquake," warned of God's judgment on Israel if the people did not turn back.

keyEvents.title: Called from the Flock
keyEvents.description: Amos was not a professional prophet or a son of a prophet, but was called by God while he was tending sheep and growing sycamore figs. He stated this clearly to the priest Amaziah in Bethel.

keyEvents.title: Judgment on the Nations
keyEvents.description: Amos prophesied God's judgment against Israel's neighboring nations—Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, and Moab—using the repeated phrase 'for three sins, even for four.' Finally, he turned his judgment toward Judah and Israel itself.

keyEvents.title: The Demand for Justice
keyEvents.description: Amos proclaimed that God rejects empty worship, festivals, and sacrifices, and instead demands that justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.

keyEvents.title: Visions of God's Judgment
keyEvents.description: Amos received a series of visions from God: locusts, fire, a plumb line, and a basket of summer fruit, all illustrating the coming judgment on Israel.

keyEvents.title: Confrontation with Amaziah
keyEvents.description: The priest Amaziah at the sanctuary in Bethel accused Amos of conspiracy against King Jeroboam and tried to drive him back to Judah. Amos stood firm on his divine calling and pronounced judgment against Amaziah.

versions.title: The Prophet of Justice
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Prophet of Righteousness' is good and descriptive, but could be expanded slightly to capture his background as a lay prophet. Suggest retaining the current title since it covers the core message.; [minor] Amos's lifespan is given as 'c. 760–750 BC', which appears to refer more to his period of activity than his actual life span. It should be clarified that this refers to his prophetic ministry, not his birth and death years.; [major] According to Amos 1:1 and 7:14, Amos was not only a prophet but also a shepherd (nōqēd) and a tender of sycamore figs (bōlēs šiqmîm). These roles should be included for completeness.; [minor] The book of Amos also contains important visions (locusts, fire, plumb line, basket of summer fruit) in chapters 7–9 that are central to the book. A key event about the visions could be added.; [major] There is a lack of footnotes covering historical, archaeological, linguistic, and theological details about Amos. These should be added.; [minor] The summary is good but could be strengthened by mentioning the context: that he ministered during King Jeroboam II's period of prosperity, and that his prophecies are dated 'two years before the earthquake' (Amos 1:1).

footnotes.text: The Hebrew word 'nōqēd' (נֹקֵד) used for Amos in 1:1 does not mean a common shepherd, but one who owns and trades livestock. The same word is used for King Mesha of Moab in 2 Kings 3:4, suggesting that Amos may have had some social status.

Amos's hometown Tekoa was located about 16 km south of Jerusalem in the Judean highlands. The city is identified with the ruin mound Khirbet Taqua, where archaeological excavations have revealed settlement traces from the Iron Age.

Amos ministered during the reign of King Jeroboam II of Israel (ca. 786–746 BC), a period of great economic prosperity and territorial expansion. Archaeological finds from Samaria, including ivory inlays and luxury items, confirm the material abundance that Amos criticized (Amos 3:15; 6:4).

The reference to the earthquake in Amos 1:1 ('two years before the earthquake') has been confirmed by archaeological evidence. Excavations at Hazor have uncovered destruction layers dated to the mid-8th century BC, which likely stem from this earthquake.

Amos's statement 'Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream' (5:24) has become one of the most quoted verses in prophetic literature and has had great influence on social ethical thinking throughout history.
In rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Makkot 24a), Amos is counted among the prophets who summarized the essence of the Torah in a single principle—the demand for justice and righteousness.
